summary:
**Flame in Freefall** is our attempt to understand something important for future space missions: how does fire behave when there is almost no gravity?

We developed an interactive platform using 100 available experimental records from NASA's FLEX combustion research. It brings together an experiment explorer, interactive charts, a 3D space environment and a simulator that compares how flames behave on Earth and in microgravity.

Through this platform, users can explore how reduced buoyancy changes flame shapes, oxygen movement and combustion behaviour. We wanted to make complex space research easier to understand through interactive visualizations rather than just presenting scientific data.

Why does this matter? Because fire safety is a major challenge for astronauts. Understanding how flames behave beyond Earth can help researchers work towards safer spacecraft and future missions to the Moon and Mars.

In the future, we also plan to expand our datasets and introduce a conceptual astronaut fire-safety suit.
details:
Flame in Freefall — Project Details

Flame in Freefall is an interactive research platform developed to explore how fire behaves in microgravity and how understanding these changes can contribute to safer human space exploration.

Our platform uses 100 available experimental records from NASA's FLEX combustion research. Users can explore experimental records, filter data, view interactive charts and understand different combustion parameters through a dedicated Experiment Explorer and Mission Control dashboard.

One of our main features is an educational combustion simulator that compares flame behaviour on Earth (1G) and in microgravity (0G). On Earth, gravity-driven buoyancy causes hot gases to rise, while in microgravity, buoyancy is greatly reduced and molecular diffusion becomes more important. Our visualizations help users understand how these differences affect flame shape, oxygen transport and combustion behaviour.

The project provides an accessible way to explore complex scientific data and supports awareness of potential fire-safety challenges in spacecraft. Our intended impact is to help researchers and space enthusiasts better understand combustion beyond Earth and contribute to research for safer future missions to the Moon and Mars.

Technology used: We developed the platform using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python with Flask. We used Three.js for 3D space visualizations, Plotly for interactive charts and CSV datasets for experimental data exploration.

What makes our project creative is the combination of scientific research, interactive data analysis, spacecraft-inspired 3D visualization and educational simulation in one platform. Instead of simply displaying research papers or datasets, we make the information easier to explore visually.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, the limitations of available experimental data, usability, accessibility and the importance of clearly distinguishing real experimental observations from educational simulations.

Future scope: We plan to integrate additional NASA datasets, expand our analysis capabilities and develop a conceptual interactive astronaut fire-safety suit to explore possible protective features for future space missions.

Our vision is simple: understanding how flames behave beyond Earth is an important step towards making future space exploration safer.
